From Crawled to Published: A Publisher-Controlled Web Architecture for an AI-Native Internet

Yixi Chen Email: yixi.chen@kaust.edu.sa    Muhammad Bilal Email: muhammad.bilal@kaust.edu.sa    Tie Ma    Zafar Ayyub Qazi Affiliation: KAUST  Beihang University  LUMS    Marco Canini    Suhaib Fahmy
Abstract

AI agents, not humans, are becoming the web’s primary consumers, yet the web still ships content structured for human browsing, with no native way for publishers to expose the semantic units within it. Access is therefore mediated by a handful of AI providers that crawl, chunk, and index content unilaterally, leaving publishers little control over how their content is represented, retrieved, or attributed. We argue this is a structural problem, not one better chunking or retrieval algorithms can solve. The web lacks a native layer for publisher-controlled semantic discovery and retrieval. We propose AISTRAL, an AI-Native Internet architecture that supplies this layer. Publishers expose semantically meaningful units (e.g., passages, claims, tables) through explicit, policy-governed interfaces they control, and a web-native semantic resolver, analogous to DNS but operating over meaning rather than location, lets agents discover relevant sources before retrieving fine-grained content directly from publishers. Our end-to-end prototype matches or exceeds representative centralized retrieval pipelines in answer quality, with up to 4.2×4.2\times higher accuracy on large, specialized document collections. Against a public web-search agent, it answers up to 4.2×4.2\times more questions correctly, while moving 2.92.9–41×41\times less data per query. Because retrieval terminates at publisher-operated servers, attribution, provenance, and usage policies travel with the content, realigning incentives across the web ecosystem.11 1 Data: https://github.com/sands-lab/aistral-dataset

1 Introduction

In 2001, Tim Berners-Lee and colleagues sketched the web’s next act: a Semantic Web whose content would carry machine-readable meaning, letting software agents traverse pages and complete tasks on their users’ behalf [29]. The vision was right about the destination and early about the vehicle. Its intended consumers were rule engines that could not interpret unstructured content, so meaning had to be formalized in advance, in standards such as RDF and OWL, and interoperation required agreeing on shared vocabularies up front. Publishers never took on that burden at scale, and the effort stalled, as its own authors later chronicled [42].

A quarter-century later, the machine consumers have arrived, just not the ones the Semantic Web was designed for. Rather than requiring publishers to encode meaning in a predefined ontology, LLM-based agents infer it from ordinary, human-oriented content as they answer a query, and they now dominate consumption of the web: as of August 2026, bots account for 60.8% of Internet traffic [12], with AI scraper traffic alone growing 597% over the past year [23]. But because the web still exposes primarily its human-facing representation, a version of the machine-readable web is being built anyway by AI providers. AI search systems construct machine-usable representations through a mix of provider-controlled crawling and query-time access [41]. Proprietary retrieval pipelines fetch pages, chunk them (split them into retrieval-sized passages), embed them (map them to vectors for similarity search), and store them in searchable indexes [2, 1, 31].

The economics are starkly asymmetric. Traditional search kept crawling and referral loosely coupled (Google’s crawl-to-refer ratio is roughly 5.2:1), whereas frontier AI companies crawl over a thousand pages for every visitor they refer back [13], and cite only a small fraction of the pages they access when generating an answer [41].22 2 For example, the study [41] finds that the GPT-5 Thinking model cites only one URL for approximately every five webpages it accesses. Publishers watch zero-click interactions erode the value their content creates [4], armed only with coarse, crawler-identity-level controls such as robots.txt and llms.txt [11]. Meanwhile, which sources are consulted, cited, or ignored is increasingly decided by a few providers [44, 45, 16, 9], introducing a new layer of centralized gatekeeping atop an originally decentralized web.

We argue these are two failures of the same missing layer. The Semantic Web asked publishers to do too much: formalize meaning up front, coupling how content is represented to how every consumer would interpret it, and it collapsed under that coordination burden. Today’s AI-mediated web asks publishers for nothing and takes everything: providers reverse-engineer semantic units from human-oriented pages lossily and unilaterally. At the same time publishers have no interface through which to express control at all. What both lack is a native web layer for publisher-controlled semantic discovery and retrieval; recent work frames AI agents as an infrastructure problem [6], and this, we argue, is the missing infrastructure.

Crucially, the consumer shift is what finally makes such a layer feasible: because LLM-based agents can interpret ordinary content without a predefined schema, publishers need only expose their content’s semantic units, not formalize their meaning for the entire world. Emerging agent protocols do not provide this layer. MCP [3] (§ 2.1.1) standardizes how an agent talks to a server it already knows, much as TCP standardizes delivery between two known endpoints. It leaves open what publishers expose, and how uncoordinated publishers become uniformly discoverable and retrievable by any agent, the same naming-and-semantics gap HTTP filled over TCP.

This paper fills this gap with AISTRAL, a hierarchical, publisher-first architecture that standardizes roles and interfaces for a semantic web at Internet scale. It completes, we argue, the Semantic Web’s journey with its coupling inverted: meaning stays with publishers, and interpretation moves to agents. Concretely, the AISTRAL AI-Native Internet is characterized by four core design principles:

  • ∙\bullet

    Publisher-Controlled Semantic Interfaces: Publishers expose queryable endpoints for the semantic units, such as passages, claims, tables, and multimodal segments, together with provenance, attribution, licensing, and access-policy metadata. The interfaces may be implemented over MCP, but AISTRAL adds what MCP leaves undefined: what publishers expose, and how uncoordinated publishers become discoverable.

  • ∙\bullet

    Semantic Discovery: A web-native semantic resolver maps an agent’s query and constraints to relevant publisher-operated endpoints using lightweight source-level records. It returns source references, not content or answers, separating source selection from content access so that no single provider controls both stages end to end.

  • ∙\bullet

    First-Class Semantic Retrieval: Retrieval of semantic units becomes a native web abstraction. Given the endpoints discovery returns, an agent queries each publisher directly and receives the units relevant to the query, without downloading or parsing full documents.

  • ∙\bullet

    Internet-Scale Efficiency: The architecture must be built to scale to the size of the web itself, not adapted to it afterwards.

These principles are realized by three independently owned roles connected by three narrow interfaces.

  • ∙\bullet

    Publishers run Agentic Twins: servers under publisher control that expose a source’s content as semantic units rather than as pages to be scraped, populated through a publish interface.

  • ∙\bullet

    Infrastructure providers run semantic resolvers, which operate analogously to DNS but over meaning rather than location: Agentic Twins register lightweight discovery records (per-source summaries and metadata, not content) through insert, and an AI agent’s resolve query returns the addresses of relevant Agentic Twins, not answers.

  • ∙\bullet

    The AI agent (the client) then invokes search against the selected Twins to retrieve fine-grained semantic units directly from publishers, and synthesizes the answer locally.

Discovery is thereby separated from retrieval: the resolver never holds content, and retrieval always terminates at a publisher-operated server. This hierarchy contrasts sharply with today’s centralized retrieval pipelines: instead of a single entity deciding how content is chunked and retrieved, responsibility is distributed across publishers, semantic resolvers, and AI agents, with clear interfaces and control boundaries (Fig. 2).

Beyond efficiency, the architecture realigns incentives across the web ecosystem. Publishers keep control over how their content is accessed, exposing semantic units through Agentic Twins they operate, while the resolver indexes only per-source discovery metadata (Fig. 2). Attribution, provenance, and usage-policy fields travel with each unit from publication to final retrieval, rather than being stripped out during centralized crawling and re-indexing (§ 5). AI developers gain cleaner, lower-latency access to structured knowledge without brittle scraping pipelines, infrastructure providers shed redundant crawler-induced load, and users receive more transparent, attributable responses. Together, these incentives suggest an adoption path built on the web’s decentralized governance rather than on unilateral cooperation from dominant AI platforms. Early industry motion supports this path: Cloudflare now builds per-publisher AI indexes with an aggregated cross-site index [8] and meters publisher compensation per crawl [10], though as single-vendor products rather than the open, interoperable layer we argue for (§ 5).

We implement and evaluate AISTRAL end-to-end against realistic baselines. footnote 4 summarizes the result: AISTRAL stays near centralized retrieval’s own data cost (∼2×\sim 2\times) while matching or exceeding its accuracy, and clearly outperforms a public web-search agent, which needs 55–80×80\times more data for mixed accuracy (§ 4).

The Semantic Web’s goal, a web AI agents can consume with publisher intent intact, no longer requires global ontological consensus. It requires rethinking who does the work of preparing content for agents, and who controls how that content is accessed. Publishers expose, resolvers discover, agents interpret, and interfaces make that division binding. Agents already approximate the applications the Semantic Web promised, composing answers from many independent sources, but they do so by scraping, without provenance, permission, or payment, and least reliably on the specialized sources where open-web search falls short (footnote 4). With such a layer, the same applications could retrieve each unit directly from its publisher, with provenance and usage terms attached and each source cited and compensated, sustaining the publishing they depend on rather than eroding it. As a vision paper grounded in a concrete system design, this work takes a first step. We introduce a publisher-first architecture, implement multiple semantic resolver designs, and evaluate them end-to-end. Challenges remain, including resolver governance, incentive-compatible deployment, trust and ranking, and retrieval and caching optimization (§ 5). We hope this work catalyzes a broader community effort toward a web that AI agents read and its publishers, at last, get to write.

2 Current AI-based Web search

In its simplest form, current AI-based web search works as follows. When a user submits a query, the AI system first performs a web search using either external search engines (e.g., Google, Bing) or a proprietary index maintained by the AI provider to identify the most relevant, high-quality sources. The system then accesses the web pages, parses each page into an ingestible format, chunks the content, and stores it in a vector database. Deployed systems already work this way: Tavily, for example, crawls web content once and serves it from its own cache for every later query [1].

The natural language query is translated into a vector embedding using an embedding model. This is used to retrieve relevant chunks from the vector database, and an LLM generates its answer based on this in-context information. This process is increasingly “agentic,” meaning the system may decompose complex questions into sub-tasks, search for each separately, and aggregate the results. If information is insufficient or ambiguity remains, the system iterates over previous steps. Additionally, knowledge graphs and keyword-based search might be incorporated for further improvement. To ensure accuracy, these systems ground responses with inline citations, enabling users to verify facts against original sources.

While this centralized architecture offers a global view of information and corresponding benefits, it has significant structural drawbacks, as depicted in  footnote 4. Because a single provider owns crawling, chunking, embedding, and indexing end-to-end, publishers have no visibility into how their content is represented internally and no means to influence it. That is, the provider alone decides every re-indexing choice, from adopting a new embedding model to changing the chunking policy for the whole corpus, no matter the compute and storage cost. This also means chunking and embedding choices stay fixed centrally, the same choices applied to every publisher’s content. Yet prior work shows the opposite is true: the best chunk size and embedding model depend on the data and domain [48, 5, 43]. This suggests that content-aware choices, made per publisher instead of once for the whole web, would perform better. The result is an architecture that blocks publisher control by design, not just by making it inconvenient: publishers have no interface to express a preference, even if the provider wanted to honor one.

There is a deeper issue underneath this: the content being chunked and embedded was never written for that purpose. Webpages are built for people to read, so they rely on narrative pacing, visual emphasis, and figures that only make sense in context. So crawling, chunking, and embedding systems have to work backward from this human-focused format, trying to recover the meaningful units and facts it contains. This process is inherently lossy and fragile, no matter how much compute or engineering effort goes into it.

We use this centralized AI-based status quo web search design as our baseline for comparison against the AISTRAL AI-Native Internet architecture.

2.1 Related Work

2.1.1 Communication Protocols.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) [3] and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) [19] standardize how two parties that already know each other exchange messages, much as TCP standardizes delivery between two endpoints that already know how to interpret each other’s bytes. Neither addresses how independent, uncoordinated publishers expose content so that any agent can uniformly discover and retrieve it. This is the same naming-and-semantics gap HTTP filled over TCP.

This gap spans both halves of AISTRAL. An Agentic Web Server is not merely an MCP server, but a role that standardizes how a publisher prepares and exposes semantic units in the first place, a question MCP leaves entirely to each server’s implementation. Also, a semantic resolver is not merely a sharper MCP registry, since the registry catalogs static, developer-published servers. It has no convention for a publisher’s dynamic corpus changes or a query narrowing that catalog by semantic relevance. These are the two halves of the contract AISTRAL standardizes (§ 3).

2.1.2 Semantic Web.

The Semantic Web [29] envisioned a web of machine-readable data through ontologies and formal metadata (RDF, OWL), later revisited by its own authors as progress stalled at web scale [42]. At its core, it assumes meanings among all documents must be formalized and agreed upon in advance, coupling how content is represented to how it is interpreted. This required global ontological consensus that proved difficult to reach, and is largely orthogonal to LLM-based agents, which interpret content flexibly at retrieval time without a predefined schema. SOLID [24] pursues a related decentralization goal but from a different angle, letting individuals own and control their personal data in self-hosted pods rather than platform silos. However, it only addresses data ownership, not publisher-side content discovery or retrieval for AI agents.

Closer to our setting, NLWeb [33] lets any website expose an MCP-backed natural-language query endpoint over its own content, reusing existing Schema.org markup as a lightweight semantic substrate55 5 This is structurally similar to an Agentic Twin’s search() in AISTRAL.. However, NLWeb provides no equivalent discovery layer. It means an agent must already know which site to query. Without such a discovery layer, it has to query every candidate site one by one, introducing exactly the uncontrolled, site-by-site search that we try to avoid. AISTRAL’s semantic resolver is precisely this missing piece: decoupling representation from interpretation as LLMs enable, while still bounding discovery at web scale.

2.1.3 Storage and Indexing.

Separately, work on storage systems targets the scale and latency demands of AI-driven retrieval. Modern vector databases demonstrate how chunk-level semantic indexing can scale to billions of items [46, 37, 25], providing the infrastructure that retrieval pipelines build upon. These works optimize how an index is stored and queried, independent of what should be indexed or who controls that decision.

2.1.4 Retrieval-Technique Optimization.

A large and active literature improves retrieval quality within a fixed pipeline. Chunking strategy is known to significantly affect retrieval quality, with optimal chunk size and boundary split varying by document type and domain [5, 48]. Embedding choice is similarly domain-sensitive, motivating works on domain-specific and task-specific embedding models [43]. Beyond flat vector similarity, knowledge-graph-augmented retrieval (GraphRAG [21]) captures entity and relational structure that pure embedding similarity can miss [15, 20]. Each of these techniques improves retrieval quality within a single, centrally-controlled pipeline. None of them ask who controls it, how content enters it, or how it stays current as sources change. AISTRAL instead exposes explicit interfaces (Appendix B), giving publishers and resolvers a defined place to handle these questions.

2.1.5 Semantic Caching.

A related line of work targets serving efficiency rather than retrieval quality directly, caching semantically similar queries or sub-results to reduce redundant computation and latency [18, 40, 47]. This is largely orthogonal to our contribution: caching can be layered atop any component, as we note in § 5.

However, each of these efforts is ad-hoc, optimizing one piece of the pipeline in isolation: agent-tool communication, index storage, retrieval quality, or serving latency. They treat the pipeline’s overall structure and ownership as fixed. Yet collaborating across components can unlock gains neither could reach alone, as shown by algorithm-system co-design work combining retrieval and generation [26]. AISTRAL instead targets the boundaries between these components: who controls content representation, how sources are discovered, and how retrieval responsibility is distributed across publishers, resolvers, and agents. We view this as complementary rather than competing: AISTRAL builds on and can incorporate all of the above: an agentic web server can use MCP to expose tools, a vector database to index its content, GraphRAG to structure it, and semantic caching to serve efficiently. In addition, AISTRAL provides the missing structural layer that determines who makes these choices, and how the results become discoverable across the open web.

3 System Architecture

3.1 Design Objectives

We introduce the concept of an AI-Native Internet, an architectural evolution of the web designed to natively support semantic retrieval, agentic workflows, and fine-grained information access. Rather than treating the web as a collection of HTML documents to crawl and parse, the AI-Native Internet exposes structured, semantically indexed interfaces optimized for LLM-based AI systems. The key design objectives for AI-Native Internet are as follows:

  • ∙\bullet

    Publisher-First Control and Incentive Alignment (O1): Website operators should retain explicit control over how their content is accessed by AI systems. This includes deciding what information is exposed, how content is structured for AI consumption, how data is chunked and where provenance, attribution, copyright signals, and usage policies attach as metadata carried through the interfaces. By shifting these decisions from centralized AI providers to publishers, the architecture enables clearer incentive alignment across publishers, AI developers, infrastructure providers, and users.

  • ∙\bullet

    Semantic Discovery (O2): Semantic discovery should be hierarchical rather than centralized. AI agents should first discover relevant information sources through a web-native semantic resolver before retrieving fine-grained content directly from publishers. This separation of source discovery from content access avoids opaque, end-to-end ranking pipelines and distributes responsibility across semantic resolvers, publishers, and agents, mirroring the Internet’s existing hierarchical design principles (e.g., DNS).

  • ∙\bullet

    AI-Native, Semantic-First Access (O3): As discussed in § 2, today’s web content is authored for human cognition, forcing AI systems to reverse-engineer semantically meaningful units (e.g., passages, claims, tables, multimodal segments) from content built for human readers. The architecture should instead treat these semantic units as a first-class, publisher-exposed abstraction with a native place to live, rather than something every consumer must independently re-derive.

  • ∙\bullet

    Efficiency and Scalability (O4): As LLM-based AI agents issue increasingly complex, multi-step queries, the architecture must scale efficiently. By enabling scoped retrieval of relevant sources and fine-grained content, the system should minimize redundant crawling, excessive bandwidth usage, and repeated re-indexing, while remaining practical to deploy and operate at Internet scale.

Together, these design objectives inform AISTRAL, a publisher-first architecture in which semantic structure and access control are embedded into the web’s content-publishing and retrieval substrate, rather than concentrated within a small number of centralized AI platforms.

3.2 System Overview

Fig. 2presents the high-level architecture of AISTRAL achieving AI-Native Internet. Rather than relying on a centralized retrieval service, AISTRAL separates content publication from query resolution through two complementary workflows.

The publication workflow allows publishers to expose semantic content while retaining full control over content preparation and hosting (O1). Publishers publish their content through agentic web servers, which perform semantic preprocessing (e.g., chunking and embedding) and register source-level metadata with the semantic resolver66 6 Throughout this paper, AISTRAL is illustrated using a deployment model where infrastructure providers host the agentic web servers. The architecture itself does not depend on this particular deployment, and alternative ownership models are discussed in § 5.. We call each such server an Agentic Twin: a publisher-controlled, queryable counterpart to a website, exposing the site’s semantic units through the search interface (§ 3.4) rather than serving pages for human browsing. This establishes a lightweight discovery layer without centralizing the underlying content.

The query-resolution workflow begins when an AI agent receives a user query. Internally, the agent is organized into two components: a retriever, which performs source discovery through the semantic resolver to identify relevant agentic web servers and then retrieves semantically relevant content directly from those sources, and a synthesizer, which synthesizes the retrieved content into a final response. This work’s contributions center on the retriever; the synthesizer follows a standard retrieval-augmented generation design. By separating source discovery from semantic retrieval, AISTRAL preserves publisher autonomy while enabling scalable and decentralized knowledge access.

3.3 Semantic Publication

The semantic publication workflow enables publishers to expose AI-consumable content while retaining ownership over content preparation, hosting, and access policies. Rather than uploading documents to a centralized index or exposing them to crawlers, publishers make semantic endpoints discoverable through lightweight source registration.

Semantic Preparation.

The publication workflow begins at , where publishers expose AI-consumable content through the publish interface on an agentic web server (O3). Rather than prescribing a fixed semantic preprocessing pipeline, AISTRAL deliberately delegates semantic preparation to content publishers, according to application requirements. This preparation may include document chunking, embedding generation, metadata extraction, or alternative semantic representations suitable for downstream retrieval. By decoupling semantic preparation from the architecture itself, AISTRAL remains agnostic to application domains and future retrieval techniques while allowing publishers to retain full control over how their content is represented and maintained.

Source Registration.

After semantic preparation, registers the published source with the semantic resolver through the insert interface. The resolver does not replicate publishers’ full prepared content or fine-grained semantic units; instead, it stores a lightweight snippet sufficient for discovery (e.g., a short content summary per source) alongside source identifiers, endpoint locations, and optional metadata. Resolve matches queries against this snippet to determine relevance, while metadata serves a different role, narrowing candidates by constraints such as freshness, domain, or policy (§ 5). Consequently, the resolver functions as a lightweight discovery layer, while the underlying knowledge remains hosted and managed by the corresponding publishers.

The registered sources subsequently become available for discovery during the query-resolution workflow, described in the following subsection.

3.4 Query Resolution

The query-resolution workflow transforms user queries into grounded responses by progressively acquiring knowledge from decentralized semantic sources. Unlike conventional retrieval architectures that couple source discovery and content retrieval within a centralized service, AISTRAL explicitly separates these two operations (O2). This separation enables AI agents to dynamically discover relevant semantic sources before retrieving knowledge directly from the corresponding agentic web servers.

Query Understanding.

The workflow begins where the AI agent submits a user query. During , the retriever interprets the query according to the application’s objectives and execution strategy. This stage may involve query rewriting, decomposition, planning, or other reasoning mechanisms prior to external knowledge acquisition.

Query decomposition itself is not a new concept. Major AI providers already do this. What AISTRAL proposes is where it happens. Today, decomposition happens inside the centralized AI provider, together with crawling and indexing. In AISTRAL, it runs on the client, as part of the retriever. No single party needs to own both decomposition and content access anymore.

Source Discovery and Semantic Retrieval.

Following query understanding, the retriever performs two sequential operations. At , it queries the semantic resolver to identify relevant semantic sources and obtain the corresponding retrieval endpoints. The retriever then invokes to retrieve semantically relevant information directly from the discovered agentic web servers. This separation enables the resolver to operate solely as a discovery service, while semantic retrieval remains fully decentralized.

Response Generation.

Once the required information has been collected, the synthesizer aggregates the retrieved data at , synthesizing the final response. Finally, the agent returns the generated response to the user. Because retrieval is performed directly against the discovered semantic sources, the synthesized response reflects the most up-to-date publisher-provided knowledge available during execution.

The full specifications of these interfaces, together with the implementations of the semantic resolver and their ingestion and query-resolution behavior, are provided in Appendix B.

4 Evaluation

Our evaluation answers four questions:

  • ∙\bullet

    Does the architecture hold up? Does separating source discovery from content retrieval reach the same answer quality as a centralized status quo pipeline that owns both?

  • ∙\bullet

    What does decentralization cost or save? How much data moves per query under AISTRAL, compared to a centralized retriever and a web-search agent (O4)?

  • ∙\bullet

    Where do errors come from? When the pipeline gets an answer wrong, is the cause routing, retrieval, or synthesis?

  • ∙\bullet

    Does this generalize? Do the answers to (1)-(3) still hold across different kinds of corpora, either small and diverse, large and repetitive, or adversarial public-web content?

Experimental Setup: We run experiments on an Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS server running in a QEMU virtualized environment, with 32 vCPUs (AMD EPYC 9754) and 64 GB RAM. We ingest each unique document exactly once and split it into passages using LangChain’s RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter [28] with a chunk size of 1,500 characters and an overlap of 150 characters; we selected this chunk size via a sweep, as smaller chunks degrade retrieval by fragmenting the statement- and table-level context that queries match against, consistent with prior findings that optimal chunk size depends on document type and content structure [5, 48]. Passages are embedded with OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model, whose unit-normalized vectors make Euclidean (L2L_{2}) and cosine ranking equivalent, and are indexed in a per-server ChromaDB collection. Documents are placed by source identity: the filing entity (company) for LOONG, or the source web domain for the URL-grounded datasets. Each identity is hashed to a single server, so all documents sharing an identity live on the same server99 9 We use SHA-256 over the identity key. We assume one content provider hosts all documents under a given identity, and that identities hash roughly uniformly across the NN servers.. A multi-hop query draws on several distinct identities (different companies or different web domains). Its evidence therefore lands on different servers, and answering it requires routing across them.

Complicated questions requiring multi-hop reasoning are decomposed into a fixed set of sub-queries that are routed independently, executed in parallel, and finally have results merged. The decomposition is single shot, so a sub-query cannot be conditioned on entities resolved by another1010 10 We do not handle “bridge” questions, where one hop finds an entity the next hop looks up. This is out of scope: our contribution is the structure, not retrieval optimization. We leave it to future work.. We deploy 10 agentic twin servers. For each sub-query, the resolver returns the semantically relevant twins (up to half of all twins) and we retrieve the top-kk chunks from each. We sweep kk (the per-server retrieval depth) in our experiments. The passages retrieved across servers are concatenated into a single context, from which gpt-5-mini synthesizes the final answer, grounded strictly on the retrieved context and not from its own internal knowledge (Appendix G). A query is scored 00 and counted as a failure when no server returns any passage (empty context), or when the synthesizer reports the retrieved passages lack the answer (irrelevant context).

Dataset: We want benchmarks that stress a decentralized resolver in different ways: how many documents a single query needs, how topically diverse or near-duplicate the corpus is, and how queries are phrased. We also want to attribute each failure to a specific stage (i.e., routing, chunk retrieval, or synthesis) rather than only scoring the final answer. The second goal requires close-ended answers, document-level gold labels, and fine-grained evidence that is localized to a few spans1111 11 We also evaluate with an open-ended dataset in Appendix D.. Three benchmarks meet the requirements: KILT-HotpotQA [38], LOONG [22], and BrowseComp+ [7]. We sample 100 queries per dataset: ingesting every query’s gold documents makes the full benchmarks too costly to run. All sampled queries share one corpus, therefore each query is still resolved against the others’ documents as distractors. Here we order them by increasing corpus adversariality.

KILT-HotpotQA is built from Wikipedia. Each question is a two-hop bridge or a comparison question grounded in exactly two gold pages, and natively ships sentence-level provenance. Evidence is thus multi-document but the corpus is topically diverse with no near-duplicate passages, isolating cross-document composition from disambiguation.

BrowseComp+ replaces BrowseComp’s live-web setting with a fixed corpus of ∼\sim100K human-verified web documents, labeling per query the evidence documents needed to answer and the gold documents that also contain the answer. These labels are document-level only; therefore we construct character-level evidence spans ourselves to support our attribution analysis (Appendix C). Its queries are long, obfuscated multi-clue puzzles spanning a broad topical mix and are the most evidence-hungry. We use a median of 6 (up to 10) evidence documents, stressing the breadth of routing over heterogeneous open-domain text.

LOONG is built from financial 10-K filings and spans single-span factual lookups (L1) and multi-span comparative questions (L2) that aggregate a metric (e.g., total operating revenue) across up to nine companies. Answering an L2 question therefore requires retrieving every required evidence span.1212 12 We use 50 L1 and 50 L2 queries: after filtering LOONG to English non-paper L1/L2 questions (Appendix C), only 75 L1 and 80 L2 qualify, and the evidence-clean L2 pool tops out near 50. Thus, we allocate 50 queries for each L1/L2 type in our testset. Each question bundles several companies’ filings. Unlike the other two datasets, the distractors here are structurally near-identical to the gold document, the same financial line items recur across companies. This makes telling similar documents apart the central retrieval challenge. Thus, for passages with near-duplicate table rows, we additionally prepend each chunk with its filing entity (company) name before embedding.

Baselines. A wrong answer from the full system has two possible causes: retrieval failed to surface the relevant document, or the synthesizer was handed the right document but still answered incorrectly. To attribute errors between these two causes, we compare against two baselines that isolate them: one that removes retrieval entirely by always giving the synthesizer perfect evidence, and another that replaces our curated retrieval with an unstructured, realistic alternative.

Centralized retrieval represents a common industry practice today (§ 2): a single provider crawls, chunks, and indexes content into one shared pipeline, the same architecture used by production systems such as Tavily [1]. We implement it with the same chunking, embedding, and synthesis setting as AISTRAL, so the two differ only in how retrieval is structured, not in model or preprocessing choices (§ A.1).

Oracle (gold docs given) isolates retrieval from reading: for each query it skips routing and chunk retrieval and feeds the full gold document(s) directly to the synthesizer, which answers with the same model and synthesis prompt as the full system and is scored with the same correctness metric. It therefore measures synthesizer performance when the relevant document is guaranteed to be in context, letting us attribute the full system’s errors to retrieval versus reading. We report each dataset at its operating retrieval depth kk: the smallest kk at which the system’s correctness plateaus (additional chunks no longer improve it).

Web search agent is the complementary, realistic baseline: it replaces the curated corpus dataset and routing with an off-the-shelf web-search agent, where the same synthesizer model (gpt-5-mini) answers each query using live public-web search (recording the pages it cites), judged with the same correctness metric. It captures what a general LLM-plus-web-search system achieves without a purpose-built semantic internet. We report the agent in a search-only, no memory configuration. It is forced to issue a web search on every query and instructed to answer only from the retrieved results, without parametric memory and without deferring via clarification.

As a robustness check, we also evaluate the agent’s default autonomous behavior, where it decides for itself whether to skip search, answer from memory, or ask for clarification, as a deployed system like ChatGPT or Perplexity. Correctness differs from the reported search-only figure by at most 4 points on any dataset, so which configuration we report does not change our conclusions (Appendix E).

Implementation Variants. We implement resolvers (for both status quo and AISTRAL) with two design variants.

  • ∙\bullet

    Base: semantic search with standard chunking and no contextualization.

  • ∙\bullet

    +Ctx: Base plus static contextualization (one LLM-generated document summary reused for all chunks from that document). Prepending LLM-generated context to chunks before embeddings is now standard practice for improving retrieval, following Anthropic’s Contextual Retrieval Technique [2].1313 13 Our +ctx variant uses one document-level summary rather than a per-chunk summary, trading some retrieval quality for a lower and more predictable ingestion cost.

We also implement and evaluate a knowledge-graph-based resolver variant; we do not report it as a main-results baseline because it is substantially costlier to ingest and our implementation did not improve correctness ( § A.2).

Document Placement Policy. Documents are sharded across nodes by a deterministic hash of a per-document source-identity key, so that documents sharing an identity colocate on one node and a multi-document query’s evidence is spread across nodes, exercising decentralized routing. We use a single policy across benchmarks and let the identity key be whatever stable handle each dataset exposes: the filing entity (company name) for LOONG, the source web domain for BrowseComp+, and the Wikipedia page identity for KILT-HotpotQA.

4.1 Correctness vs. Retrieval Traffic

Deeper retrieval improves correctness, up to a plateau. footnote 8 (top) shows correctness rising with retrieval depth kk and then flattening; we report each dataset at this plateau (shaded), indicating the smallest depth beyond which more chunks no longer help. There, AISTRAL comes close to the perfect-document-retrieval ceiling. That is, once kk is large enough, retrieval is rarely the bottleneck.

It is worth noting LOONG L2 is an exception: AISTRAL exceeds perfect-retrieval baseline (0.630.63 vs. 0.470.47), because the full L2 gold context is simply too large for the synthesizer, the synthesis component introduced in § 3.2 ( in Fig. 2). LOONG’s filings are far bigger than the other corpora (median ∼\sim150 KB, vs. ∼\sim11 KB Wikipedia pages), and an L2 comparison query draws on a median of three of them at once (∼\sim87 K tokens, up to 292292 K). The enormous context size is enough to overrun the synthesizer’s input limit1414 14 gpt-5-mini accepts up to ∼\sim272 K input tokens [36]. for one query on gold documents alone, leading to context confusion [32, 30]. In AISTRAL, chunk retrieval sidesteps this by feeding the synthesizer only the relevant spans. We omit the perfect-retrieval curve for LOONG L2 from footnote 8: because the gold context itself induces context confusion, it no longer functions as a meaningful upper bound.

AISTRAL beats both baselines, and the gap grows with corpus difficulty. Against a status quo retriever, AISTRAL performs roughly on par on KILT, clearly ahead on BrowseComp+, and dominant on LOONG (three-to-four times more accurate on both levels). Against a web-search agent over the public web, the margin depends on whether the answer is publicly available: on KILT (Wikipedia trivia) the agent nearly matches AISTRAL, but drops sharply on LOONG and BrowseComp+. LOONG’s drop is largely source disagreement, not retrieval failure, where the public web often has multiple defensible figures for the same metric (§ E.2). BrowseComp+ is different: it is built so no single public page carries all the clues to answer the query (§ E.3).

The cause is common to both comparisons: routing shrinks the pool each query must search. A status quo or public-web retriever ranks the evidence against the whole collection, so on a large, internally repetitive corpus the right chunks are buried among many look-alikes and fall out of the top-kk. Fig. 4 makes this concrete at the level of individual queries. For each query, we track the rank of the single best-ranked chunk containing any part of its evidence, and plot its CDF under both routing schemes. On LOONG and BrowseComp+, status quo’s curve trails AISTRAL’s by orders of magnitude in rank, where a sizable fraction of queries see no relevant chunk at all until rank 10210^{2}–10310^{3}, further away from any kk in footnote 8. On KILT the two curves nearly overlap, matching the negligible gap we report there. This gap is measured under vector-based semantic retrieval specifically, and with stronger retrieval technique, including reranking, hybrid search, or GraphRAG, could narrow it for both AISTRAL and the status quo alike.

A larger, unified index doesn’t simply transfer to “more information available”. Retrieval capacity is a bounded resource that gets consumed by corpus pool size and topical density. So a single index spanning all documents can be a strictly harder search problem than several smaller, disjoint ones [39, 14]. Instead, AISTRAL confines each query to the twin(s) hosting its documents, so the evidence surfaces easier. The effect is small on a small, diverse corpus (KILT) and largest on LOONG’s near-templated filings, where every document contributes similar-looking sections.

Contextual chunking tracks base. The dashed AISTRAL(+ctx) curves in footnote 8 stay close to base on every panel, achieving comparable correctness at a slightly higher traffic cost. Both variants clearly outperform the web-search agent everywhere except KILT, where correctness scores saturate quickly across all implementations. We therefore carry base as the default and revisit what +ctx reveals about the metric itself in § 4.2.

The accuracy costs more traffic, but far less than an open-web agent. The correctness boost doesn’t come free: retrieval traffic grows with kk (footnote 8, bottom), so operating at the plateau rather than the deepest kk keeps data movement near its minimum for a given accuracy. Even so, AISTRAL requires far less data movement than the web agent. For example, on LOONG L2 it transfers only ∼\sim0.15 MB per query at the operating kk, roughly 40×40\times less than the agent. The public web is thus both less accurate on specialized corpora and far more bandwidth-hungry; a curated, routed index answers the same queries with a fraction of the data.

4.2 Where queries fail and where correctness diverges

§ 4.1showed AISTRAL overall accuracy and cost; this section asks why. We break each query into its retrieval and answering stages to find where correctness is lost, and check whether high correctness always means retrieval worked.

Fig. 5traces each query through the pipeline, stage by stage. Routing and gold-document retrieval saturate (∼100%{\sim}100\% on every benchmark), so neither is the bottleneck1515 15 We do not evaluate how routing accuracy degrades as the number of twins grows, for budget and time concerns. § 5 discusses this as an open scaling question.. The loss concentrates at one stage: recall, the fraction of required evidence retrieved (Appendix C).

It falls to 4040–60%60\% on the LOONG L2 and KILT, and to 80% on BrowseComp+. Getting the right document is easy; getting every needed passage into the top-kk is where retrieval falls short1616 16 Not specific to our method: replacing dense embeddings with BM25 or a knowledge-graph retriever (§ A.2) performed worse, not better. BM25 missed ≈20%\approx 20\% more required passages, and the KG retriever answered LOONG questions correctly ≈18×\approx 18\times less often. Decomposition, entity-name prefixing, and twin-scoped search help instead..

Correctness diverges from recall, but behaves differently across datasets. Final correctness is shaped by two separable factors: how effectively the pipeline retrieves the required evidence, and how much the synthesizer can independently answer from its own parametric knowledge, regardless of what retrieval supplies. To isolate the second factor, we run a closed-book ablation: withholding all retrieved context and scoring what the synthesizer answers from parametric knowledge alone (implementation and full breakdown in Appendix F). This lets us categorize each dataset by how it can be answered short of complete, correct retrieval.

  • ∙\bullet

    Retrieval-required (BrowseComp+): closed-book correctness is near zero. This means the answer cannot be guessed or recalled without retrieval. Correctness is retrieval-bound.

  • ∙\bullet

    Guessable-by-elimination (LOONG L2): closed-book correctness is also near zero, so the synthesizer cannot be recalling the figures from memory. But the question itself narrows the answer space: a comparison of the form “among A, B, C, who had the highest X?” only has as many possible answers as candidates named in the question. Even with incomplete retrieval it often lands on the right one: in 70% of these cases the winning company’s name already appears in a retrieved passage, so it reads the answer off rather than computing it (the same single-hop artifact as KILT); in the remaining 30% it has neither the values nor the name and simply guesses correctly among the few candidates. Correctness thus runs ahead of recall with no memory involved.

  • ∙\bullet

    Answerable-from-memory (KILT): closed-book correctness is high (67%), since HotpotQA is sourced from Wikipedia and much of it is answerable from parametric knowledge alone. Pipeline correctness (0.860.86) is only ∼\sim19 points above this ceiling, so retrieval is adding comparatively little. Unlike LOONG L2’s candidate-constrained guessing, KILT’s multi-hop questions can be solved by two additional shortcuts: a well-documented single-hop artifact, where the answer text appears in one retrieved passage even though not every annotated bridge hop was fetched [34, 27] (76%); and, more directly, cases where the final hop is never retrieved at all and the synthesizer supplies it from memory (24%).

LOONG L1 falls outside this categorization: retrieval is already saturated, so there is no divergence to explain: the gap to correctness (98% →\rightarrow 79%) is entirely synthesis error.

5 Discussion

Governance of the Semantic Resolver: Who operates and governs the semantic resolver remains an open question. Unlike DNS, semantic resolution raises new challenges around trust, transparency, and ranking bias, and whether it is run by a consortium, federated providers, or a decentralized network will fundamentally affect neutrality and adoption. Viable designs would require auditable response logs, transparent ranking signals, and open evaluation frameworks to detect bias, abuse, or capture. Industry is already heading in this direction: Cloudflare’s AI Index pairs per-publisher indexes with an aggregated cross-site Open Index [8], and Pay Per Crawl [10] mechanizes publisher compensation, validating the incentive-alignment premise behind O1. These, however, remain single-vendor layers rather than an open standard, and the Open Index both discovers and serves content, whereas AISTRAL’s resolver is content-free by contract, with retrieval terminating at the publisher.

Hybrid Centralized–Decentralized Retrieval: A separate drawback of AISTRAL’s design is latency: multi-stage retrieval (resolve, then fetch from each source) is inherently slower than querying one centralized index. A hybrid design can trade some decentralization for speed, indexing recent or frequently-queried content centrally as a cache while the rest stays at the Agentic Twins, keeping publisher control as the default while meeting latency demands for hot content.

Where Trust Enters the Pipeline: Resolver vs. Agent: Semantic retrieval naturally splits into two stages, and trust interacts with both. The resolver returns semantically relevant sources, and may attach provenance metadata and basic trust indicators (e.g., who operates the site, source reputation, and abuse or spam signals [17]). AI agents then query the Agentic Twins for fine-grained chunks and may re-rank across sources and chunks using recency, safety filters, and application-specific policies. Separating source-level retrieval from client-side re-ranking exposes a diverse candidate pool rather than a single opaque ranking, enabling independent auditing and alternative trust strategies while preserving application control over final ordering.

From Advisory Metadata to Enforceable Provenance: Publisher-supplied attribution metadata (source, authorship, timestamp) already travels end-to-end, from insert() into the resolver’s store and back to the agent at search time, but only as advisory, uninterpreted fields. Nothing is cryptographically signed or verified, and the copyright and usage-policy fields are not yet populated or enforced. Making these signals trustworthy is future work: semantic chunks must carry verifiable provenance, including lineage, signatures, and machine-readable attribution, and publishers need standardized ways to express usage constraints that resolvers can enforce. Balancing flexible developer access with strong protection of intellectual property at Internet scale remains an open challenge.

Correctness Is Not Binary on the Public Web: Our correctness metric assumes each query has a single gold answer. That holds by construction in a curated corpus, but not on the public web. Our failure analysis (§ E.2) shows the web-search agent often finds the right entity but reports a different, defensible value, e.g., a GAAP figure instead of an adjusted one, or an original filing instead of a later restatement. Each is “correct” relative to a different authoritative source, so the metric records a failure where there is really an ambiguity. AISTRAL narrows this problem rather than solving it. Retrieving only from publisher-registered sources limits which documents can conflict, and provenance tells the agent where a number came from, a precondition for judging trust. But deciding which of two authoritative numbers is right lies beyond what routing or registration alone can guarantee.

Publisher Incentives and Operator Buy-in: Adoption asks website operators to restructure their content, so they need clear incentives. Some are direct: lower bandwidth from serving compact semantic units instead of full pages, better visibility and attribution in AI-mediated interfaces, richer analytics on how agents consume content, and the ability to charge AI providers for access through the Twins they operate, offsetting zero-click losses. These incentives are only as sound as the mechanisms beneath them: if the resolver deduplicates near-identical content from distinct publishers, the collapsed publisher loses credit and attribution despite being a legitimate source, so deduplication must be incentive-compatible, not an afterthought. Adoption also needs tooling that lets publishers convert existing sites into AI-native representations, control chunk boundaries and metadata, and attach provenance and policy signals without a full redesign. Ultimately, we believe producing content with AI consumption in mind from the outset will become essential in the age of AI-based search.

Scaling to the Web: Our implementation uses a single semantic resolver over 10 Agentic Twin servers. Internet scale raises open problems at both the resolver and the routing layer. No single resolver instance can index the entire web, so the resolver itself must be sharded hierarchically like DNS, from top-level knowledge domains down to specialized sub-domains. At the routing layer, orders of magnitude more Twins increase the chance that a query’s evidence fragments across servers, and which Twin should host which document is itself unsolved: our placement policy (§ 4) is a testbed hash, not a deployment policy. Neither problem is exotic. Partitioning, placement, and delegated resolution are classic distributed-systems problems, and DNS solved their naming analogues at Internet scale. What is genuinely open is whether those solutions survive the shift from exact-match to semantic resolution, where a query has no unique home and shard boundaries are soft.

Coexistence with the Existing Web: The architecture must integrate with current HTTP infrastructure, CDNs, and publishing workflows, letting publishers expose semantic chunks alongside existing HTML without disrupting legacy traffic. In our vision, HTML pages remain the primary representation for human browsing while semantic manifests and chunk APIs provide a parallel view for LLMs and agents; how these dual representations coevolve with traditional web search will shape the long-term impact of an AI-Native Internet.

6 Conclusion

The web’s dominant consumers are no longer the human readers it was built for. We have argued that the resulting dysfunction, crawling without permission and answers without attribution, is an architectural problem rather than a retrieval problem, and that the fix is a move from a crawled web to a published one. AISTRAL makes that move concrete. Publishers expose semantic units through Agentic Twins they control, resolvers answer discovery queries without ever holding content, and AI agents retrieve only the units they need, directly from sources. Our prototype shows the design is competitive as well as principled. It matches or exceeds centralized retrieval, and answers up to 4.2×4.2\times more questions correctly than a web-search agent while moving 2.92.9–41×41\times less data per query. AISTRAL is a first effort, deliberately so: a small set of roles and interfaces and one workable instantiation, not a finished standard. The problems that remain, resolver governance, trust and ranking, incentive-compatible deployment, and placement at scale, are larger than any single group, and they are the familiar problems of any young discovery layer, whose analogues DNS faced at a similar age. The Semantic Web supplied the ambition a quarter-century ago, and LLMs have now supplied the consumer. We offer AISTRAL as a concrete starting point, and invite the community to refine its interfaces, contest its design choices, and build the publisher-controlled layer the web now needs.
