Appendix A Implementation of Centralized AI-based Websearch

In this paper we consider two different implementations of the centralized AI-based web search. A semantic search based implementation and a Knowledge Graph based implementation.

A.1 Semantic Search based Centralized AI web search

In a semantic search based design, all web data resides in a single semantic search entity that maintains a vectorized version of the entire web. The user’s query is sent to this web-scale vector database, which returns the most relevant t​o​pktop_{k} pieces of information.

There are two main functions of a semantic resolver: ingestion and query resolution. Our implementation of the processes for ingestion and query resolution are shown in Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2, respectively.

Ingestion Flow

The ingestion works by chunking, embedding, and then storing the data from the web servers in a unified vectorDB instance.

Query Resolution

When a user submits a query, the semantic resolver performs semantic search using the vectorDB. The relevant filters are applied while performing the search and the t​o​pktop_{k} relevant chunks are retrieved and returned to the LLM/user in response. Query resolution process can also take a request to return more context around the return chunks. This can be quite useful for more complex queries.

A.2 KG based Centralized AI web search

The KG-based semantic resolver combines graph traversal with vector search to retrieve the most relevant pieces of information.

The process for ingestion and query resolution are shown in Algorithm 3 and Algorithm 4, respectively.

Ingestion Flow

The ingestion process works by first extracting the graph of entities and relations per document. This graph is then merged into a Global Knowledge Graph. Each node in the graph stores associated doc_ids for all the documents that the entity is present in. Each document is then chunked, the chunks are converted into embeddings and are stored in a vectorDB along with the metadata for each chunk that also includes the doc_id that the chunk belongs to.

Query Resolution

During the query resolution process, entities are extracted from the query. All the related nodes in the global knowledge graph are extracted via nn-hop traversal. The doc_ids in the nodes are then used to create a filter for vector search that retrieves semantically similar chunks.

Appendix B Interface Specification

AISTRAL separates publication, discovery, and retrieval into distinct interfaces so that publishers, semantic resolvers, and AI agents each retain a clear responsibility boundary. At a high level, publishers expose content and metadata for semantic preparation, semantic resolvers support source discovery over source-level representations, and agentic web servers support fine-grained retrieval over local semantic units.

publish(content, metadata)

The publish interface captures the publisher-facing side of the architecture. Its purpose is to hand content and basic source metadata to an agentic web server, which can then prepare local semantic representations for retrieval. Conceptually, this is where publisher control enters the system: content is not first crawled and reformatted by a centralized search provider, but rather provided together with metadata chosen by the publisher or content operator.

For the purposes of the design, the most important fields are shown in  Table 1. These fields express the source identity, the content itself, and the minimal metadata needed for provenance, freshness, and modality-aware handling. Additional fields such as licensing or access policy are natural extensions, but are not essential to the core interface decomposition described in this paper.

insert(documents)

The insert interface registers content records with the semantic resolver. Its role is to make content discoverable without requiring the resolver to serve the content itself. In this sense, insert is a source-registration interface rather than a user-facing retrieval interface. The argument name documents is retained for readability, but what matters architecturally is that each item carries enough semantic and metadata information to support source discovery and filtering, as listed in Table 2.

Behavior.

AISTRAL supports two resolver realizations that differ in how registered sources are indexed: a vector-based resolver and a knowledge-graph (KG) based resolver. The two share the same insert interface but populate different indices at ingestion time; their query-time behavior is described under resolve.

Vector-based ingestion. A crawler crawls the agentic web servers and generates a summary (e.g., using an LLM) of each crawled document or file. The summary is vectorized using an embedding model and inserted into a vector database, along with metadata about the agentic twin that holds the chunks of the corresponding document. The resolver therefore stores only source-level summaries rather than the underlying content, keeping it a lightweight discovery layer (Algorithm 5).

Context-enriched (+ctx) ingestion. The +ctx variant refines the vector-based path with static, document-level context on the chunk representations served for cross-document disambiguation. Each document is summarized once with an LLM, and that summary is prepended verbatim to every chunk of the document before the chunk is embedded and stored; the summary is cached per document, so enrichment costs a single LLM call per document regardless of its chunk count. A more fine-grained alternative would generate context dynamically per chunk, tailoring the prepended summary to each chunk rather than sharing one document-level summary across all of them. This would likely yield better retrieval accuracy, but it requires a separate LLM invocation for every chunk, each conditioned on the full source document, multiplying ingestion cost and latency; we therefore adopt the static document summary as a deliberate cost/quality compromise and leave dynamic, chunk-tailored context to future work. This step reuses the document summary sjs_{j} already computed in Algorithm 5 and requires no change to the query path.

KG-based ingestion. An LLM extracts entities and relations per document and creates a mini knowledge graph. Mini KGs are merged into a global KG, with nodes updated to include the server_url of the agentic web server that holds the relevant chunks. Documents are also summarized and the embeddings of their summaries are inserted into the vector database, so that graph traversal and vector similarity can be combined at query time (Algorithm 6).

resolve(query, filters)

The resolve interface is the discovery or control-plane interface. Its purpose is not to return answer content, but to identify the sources that should be queried next.

As shown in Table 3, queries in AISTRAL are accompanied by optional constraints that let the client narrow source discovery by domain, topic, language, or freshness.

Behavior.

resolve takes a query and returns the addresses of the agentic web sources holding semantically relevant data, applying the metadata-based filters above (data format, copyright, timeliness, quality, etc.) when selecting sources. Its behavior mirrors the two ingestion variants introduced under insert.

Vector-based resolution. The resolver holds a global index over the vectorized summaries of the documents it knows about. A query is matched against this index via document-level semantic similarity, and the resulting set of relevant source URLs is returned to the AI agent, which then queries those agentic web servers directly through search and synthesizes an answer from the retrieved chunks (Algorithm 7). The +ctx variant leaves this path unchanged: it issues the same query against the same index. The only difference is that the chunks later retrieved through search carry their document’s prepended summary.

KG-based resolution. Vector similarity alone does not capture relationships between entities within or across documents and may miss information that depends on relational structure rather than surface similarity. Extending the resolver with a KG layer that encodes entities and their relations enables more structured, multi-hop resolution, and provides a natural mechanism for embedding constraints into discovery, such as restricting retrieval to specific entities, relations, sources, time ranges, or publisher-defined policies. At query time, entities are extracted from the query using an LLM and expanded via nn-hop traversal; server URLs recovered from the node metadata are combined with the t​o​pktop_{k} URLs from vector-based search over the document summaries, and the union is returned (Algorithm 8).

We implement this KG layer but report the vector-based resolver as our system: on our benchmarks it did not improve retrieval accuracy over vector similarity, and was substantially worse on LOONG. The failure is structural:

  • •

    The answer is not a node. Our queries resolve to specific quantitative facts stated at single points within long narrative filings (∼66%{\sim}66\% of LOONG gold answers are numeric values). LLM entity–relation extraction captures the narrative’s entities but not these numeric statements, so the graph does not hold the evidence the query needs.

  • •

    Merges collide on repetitive corpora. Across many structurally similar filings, extracted entities and relations overlap, so merging the mini-KGs fuses or fragments nodes and traversal cannot discriminate which source to return.

  • •

    Queries link unreliably to nodes. A natural-language query rarely matches the surface form of an extracted node, so traversal misses. Vector similarity is robust to this paraphrase gap.

  • •

    It costs more for less. Per-document extraction and global merge are expensive at ingest, and graph traversal is slower at query time.

The KG layer’s value in our setting is therefore its support for structured constraints (entity, relation, source, time, and policy filters), not retrieval accuracy.

search(query, limit)

The search interface is the retrieval or data-plane interface exposed by an agentic web server. After a resolver identifies relevant sources, the AI agent uses this interface to retrieve semantically relevant units from a selected source. Unlike resolve, this interface returns content-bearing objects rather than source references.

Table 4shows the fields that matter most for understanding this design. The interface may also return auxiliary local metadata for provenance, interpretability, and implementation-level inspection.

Behavior.

Through search, agentic web servers act as queryable data sources for AI agents: in addition to serving webpages, a server receives a query and replies with the most relevant t​o​pktop_{k} semantic units, and makes all types of information searchable, including images, documents, audio, video, and databases. Because data providers understand their own data better than a centralized system, they retain full control over how content is chunked, embedded, and returned in response to a query, which enables more relevant results while preserving complete data sovereignty. This control also opens new business models: data providers can monetize their content by charging commercial AI agents for access while potentially offering free access to human users.

B.1 AI-Agent Internal Interfaces.

In addition to the cross-component interfaces above, the AI agent performs two internal operations that are architecturally important for end-to-end behavior: query processing before retrieval and answer synthesis after retrieval. These are not public network APIs, but they materially affect how user intent is translated into retrieval actions and how retrieved evidence is converted into a final answer.

process_query(q)

The process_query interface transforms a user query into a retrieval-oriented representation. Its role is to surface implicit constraints, reduce ambiguity, and produce query forms that are easier for downstream discovery and retrieval components to use effectively. Depending on the task, this stage may expose comparison scope, identify implied constraints, decompose a complex request into multiple subqueries, rephrase the request into a more retrieval-friendly form, or anonymize sensitive information before retrieval. In the evaluation setting, this interface is especially important for under-specified queries, such as comparison questions among a fixed range of companies statistics in LOONG benchmark.

Behavior.

While a user query can in principle be used directly for discovery, processing it first improves efficiency and effectiveness and can reduce exposure of Personally Identifiable Information (PII). Processing comprises one or more of:

  • ∙\bullet

    decomposition of a complex query into simpler subqueries — possibly iteratively, so that an answered subquery can further decompose or disambiguate the remainder;

  • ∙\bullet

    anonymization to remove PII; and

  • ∙\bullet

    rephrasing to remove ambiguity and optimize for search.

Processing also extracts the functional requirements implicit in free-form text and turns them into filters for downstream discovery. For example, intent classification narrows the agentic web sources worth searching. A factoid lookup needs few retrievals, whereas a qualitative analysis needs deeper research. A query can also target a specific modality such as video or image. Likewise, a freshness requirement extracted from the query maps onto the timestamp filters exposed by resolve.

synthesize(query, context)

The synthesize interface converts retrieved evidence into a final answer. Given a query and retrieved context, synthesize combines relevant semantic units, resolves partial or conflicting evidence, and produces the final grounded answer.

Extensions and Open API Work

The interfaces above capture the core architectural decomposition of AISTRAL, but they do not yet constitute a complete production protocol suite. Several extensions remain important future work, including explicit update and deletion semantics, richer policy and licensing metadata, stronger provenance and capability descriptors in resolve, access control and authorization, pagination or continuation for long retrieval results, and standardized error schemas. These additions are important for deployment and interoperability, but are orthogonal to the main architectural point of the design: separating publication, registration, discovery, and fine-grained retrieval into explicit interfaces with distinct responsibilities.

Semantic caching.

Any Internet-scale deployment of AISTRAL will require caching. Because the architecture exposes distinct interfaces, caching is naturally layered: it can be applied at process_query (processed queries and subqueries), at resolve (discovered source sets), and at search (retrieved semantic units). Query decomposition and rephrasing further increase hit rates by exposing shared subqueries across complex requests. Prior work such as Cortex [40], Category-Aware Semantic Caching [47], and domain-specific embedding models [18] provides a foundation, but a full treatment of cache placement, invalidation, and freshness across these layers is left to future work.

Appendix C Query Preprocess

We map all three benchmarks onto a single evaluation interface: each query is reduced to a question, a set of gold documents, and one or more gold-evidence spans expressed as file-level character offsets (doc, char_start, char_end) into the materialized document text. The retrieval corpus is the union of the evaluated queries’ documents. The benchmarks differ in how much of the original datasets supply this evaluation interface natively, so the preprocessing effort differs accordingly (as shown in Table 7). KILT ships evidence natively, whereas LOONG and BrowseComp+ require us to construct it, and LOONG additionally requires rewriting its questions.

C.1 KILT-HotpotQA

Selection is deterministic. We take the dev split and recover each question’s bridge/comparison type by joining on instance id (according to the original HotpotQA release), then seed-sample a balanced 50/50 set. Questions are used verbatim. Each gold Wikipedia page is materialized from the KILT knowledge source where a page’s body is stored as a list of paragraph strings; we join that list into one contiguous text file (one page →\rightarrow one document).

Gold evidence is native: KILT provenance gives paragraph-relative offsets (paragraph_id, char), which we rebase to file-level offsets by prefix-summing paragraph lengths, 𝑐ℎ𝑎𝑟​_​𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑡=∑i<p|paragraphi|+c\mathit{char\_start}=\sum_{i<p}\lvert\text{paragraph}_{i}\rvert+c. A query carries all its provenance spans (2–8 per question).

C.2 LOONG

Filtering.

From the 1,600 LOONG questions we keep English rows, drop the paper type, and drop Levels 3–4, leaving 75 Level-1 and 80 Level-2 questions, all over financial 10-K filings.

Query transformation.

Most Level-2 questions are comparative aggregations whose company set is implicit — present only in the filings bundled with the question (“the documents above”). To make them answerable under open retrieval, we deterministically rewrite such questions by prepending the candidate entity list, “Among the following candidate companies: AA, BB, …”, where the entities are extracted from the bundled document identifiers. The rewrite is rule-based and applies only to the underspecified comparative templates. For the Practical web search baseline only, we additionally qualify each LOONG question with its reporting period (fiscal year 2024, recovered from the filing identifiers).

Evidence construction.

LOONG provides no evidence spans, so we build them. A natural alternative would be handing the documents to an LLM and having it mark the evidence directly. However, this is infeasible at LOONG’s scale: the corpus for these queries is several million tokens (∼\sim20×\times a 272K-token input window), and even a single query’s bundled filings (2–9 documents) average ∼136{\sim}136K tokens and exceed the input context window cap for 12% of queries. Moreover, LLMs are unreliable at emitting exact character offsets over long documents due to context confusion. We therefore use a staged pipeline in which a heuristic step narrows down the evidence search range. Stage 1 localizes candidate windows heuristically (metric-term and answer-value matches) within each document; a triage step accepts confident rows. The remaining rows escalate to Stage 2, a bounded LLM pass (gpt-5-mini) over only the disputed slices; a final deterministic step recovers exact spans by matching the extracted evidence text back into the source document to resolve the dispute. Finally, because the bundled filings are structurally near-identical, at ingest we prefix each passage with its source company name so the retriever can disambiguate otherwise-similar rows.

C.3 BrowseComp+

Selection.

BrowseComp+ exposes no per-query domain metadata, neither from the original BrowseComp dataset, so we recover a primary domain per query using an eleven-bucket taxonomy interpreted from BrowseComp’s published category distribution [35], labeling by the answer-seeking target rather than incidental clues. We then stratified-sample the evaluation slice to match the original BrowseComp topic distribution [35]. Questions are used verbatim.

Documents and evidence.

The benchmark supplies gold documents and document-level evidence labels; it does not supply character-level evidence spans, which we construct with a heuristic locator (numeric and reverse-clue matching) that falls back to an LLM (gpt-5-mini) on hard rows, with handling for answers that recur across a document. It is worth noting that BrowseComp+ also ships curated distractor documents; because these cannot be verified as non-contributing, we treat them as optional inputs and exclude them from the evaluated corpus rather than labeling them hard negatives.

Answer-repeat deduplication.

BrowseComp+’s corpus deliberately repeats each answer across multiple documents (median 2 copies per query, up to 10), so retrieving every labeled copy is a stricter requirement than retrieving the answer itself. Any single copy is sufficient to answer the query. We therefore score recall as satisfied once any one copy is retrieved, rather than requiring all of them. This changes the reported recall rate (§ 4.2) from 44% under the stricter, all-copies criterion to 80% under the corrected one; end-to-end correctness (79%) is unaffected, since it depends only on the final answer, not on which copy was retrieved.

Appendix D Evaluation with Open-ended Queries

We also evaluate AISTRAL on LLMs-and-Web [41], a benchmark of open-ended natural-language web queries. It contains a wild variety of queries, ranging from short pointer-style lookups (e.g., locating a site’s official page) to informational questions. Each query is grounded in a set of real web documents and their source URLs harvested from the query’s prompt and from web search. Unlike our closed-ended benchmarks, its queries have no single gold answer, so correctness cannot be scored against a localized evidence span. We therefore judge each of the 50 evaluated queries with an LLM along three reference-free axes: correctness (factual accuracy and plausibility), completeness (coverage of what the query asks), and focus (staying on-topic and concise). As a reference point, we run the dataset’s gold answers (produced by the model Opus) through the same judge and axes. We mark the baseline score as a dashed line in Fig. 6, so crossing it means matching the reference answers under the same grader. This setting complements our main results by testing whether decentralized routing and synthesis hold up when answers are open-ended and graded on quality.

All variants clear the Opus baseline on every axis by k≈2k{\approx}2 and then flatten. That is, AISTRAL saves the most traffic for the same quality. We report this in the appendix rather than the main results for two reasons. First, the open-ended scores are hard to read as retrieval signal: the axes saturate near their capability once a few relevant chunks are fetched. There the differences between variants are dominated by judge noise, with no principled meaning to attach to, say, a completeness of 0.900.90 versus 0.850.85.

Second, and more importantly, this benchmark has no localized gold evidence, so we cannot run the stage-by-stage attribution of § 4.2: when a query scores low we cannot tell whether routing, span retrieval, or synthesis is at fault. As that section shows, the end-to-end score conflates the retriever and the reader; without intermediate signals it is not a debuggable measure of AISTRAL itself, which is exactly why our main evaluation uses closed-ended benchmarks with span-level gold.

Appendix E Web Search Agent Baseline

E.1 Configurations

The web-search agent baseline answers each benchmark query with the same synthesizer model used throughout the paper (gpt-5-mini), equipped with a live web-search tool (the OpenAI Responses web_search tool). It receives no benchmark corpus and no routing (only the query and the public web) and is scored with the identical reference-anchored correctness judge applied to every other system. For each query we record the pages the agent cites and their sizes, giving the per-query traffic figures reported in the main text. All runs use the same 100-query subset per benchmark as the retrieval systems.

We evaluate two configurations, differing only in when the agent searches and what it may answer from:

  • ∙\bullet

    Search-only (no memory): the configuration reported in the main results. The web-search tool is forced on every query (via tool_choice), and the agent is instructed to answer using only the retrieved results, not to fall back on parametric knowledge, and to commit to a single answer rather than requesting clarification. This mirrors the retrieval systems, which likewise retrieve and then answer every query, isolating the quality of open-web retrieval from the model’s latent knowledge.

  • ∙\bullet

    Autonomous: the agent’s default deployed behavior. The tool is offered, but the model decides for itself whether to invoke it. It may answer directly from parametric memory, and it may reply with a clarification request instead of an answer. This reflects how a shipped assistant (e.g., ChatGPT or Perplexity) behaves.

Search behavior. Under the autonomous configuration, the agent produces a substantive answer on 82% of queries (the remainder are clarification requests or errors); of those answers, 83% are grounded in at least one cited page and 17% are given from parametric memory with no citation. The memory-only fraction is highly benchmark-dependent: 32% of answers on KILT-HotpotQA but only 3% on LOONG. Tracking the closed-book results of  Appendix F: KILT questions are largely answerable from parametric knowledge, whereas LOONG’s micro-cap financial figures are not. The search-only configuration, by construction, searches on essentially every query (cited-source rate 96–100%) and never defers.

The exact system/tool prompts for both configurations are given in  Appendix G and are not reproduced here.

Effect on correctness. Forcing search and forbidding memory changes correctness within 4 points on any benchmark, as shown in  Table 8:

The two configurations therefore agree to within noise, and our conclusions do not depend on which one is reported.

E.2 Failure Analysis on LOONG

To verify that the low practical-web-search scores on LOONG (footnote 8) reflect a genuine retrieval limitation rather than a question-phrasing artifact, we audit the baseline’s failures at both levels.

L1 failure mode (0.17). On the 38/50 zero-scored queries, the agent reliably identifies the correct company but reports the wrong figure. We identify three recurring sources of disagreement:

  • ∙\bullet

    Conflicting sources: the original 10-K, a later 10-K/A restatement, GAAP vs. adjusted figures, and third-party aggregators (e.g., Macrotrends, StockAnalysis, WSJ) each report a different value for the same nominal metric.

  • ∙\bullet

    Corporate actions: reverse stock splits and share-count changes swing per-share figures by orders of magnitude. For example, AIM ImmunoTech’s Basic EPS is −$0.12-\$0.12 in the gold filing vs. −$30.92-\$30.92 reported on the open web.

  • ∙\bullet

    Metric-definition scope: For example, “administrative expenses” is $10,135K\$10,135K in the gold filing but $76,306K\$76,306K on the web, summing continuing and discontinued operations. “Capital surplus” is conflated with the web’s “additional paid-in capital.”

Even with the fiscal year added to each query, the agent cannot choose among several disagreeing public figures. Only retrieval over the authoritative filing itself resolves this, which underlines the importance of source provenance.

L2 failure mode (0.50). L2 compounds the L1 problem: a comparison across up to nine companies requires the correct per-company figure for each of them, so any single L1-style error can flip the comparison. L2 nonetheless scores higher than L1 because comparative correctness is partly robust to individual numeric noise. The relative ordering across companies can still be right even when the exact values are not.

E.3 Failure Analysis on BrowseComp+

BrowseComp+ questions are conjunctive “needle” queries: they identify a single person, place, work, or title through several oblique constraints that must all hold simultaneously. For example, “in a pre-2023 literary work by an author whose parent was the first professor of a field in their country, the protagonist is originally from [place]…” (gold: Rebecca). The web-search agent scores low here (0.39 autonomous / 0.38 search-only). Its 63 failures in the search-only configuration split into two roughly equal patterns:

  • ∙\bullet

    Retrieval miss (non-answer): 33/6333/63. Even when forced to search, the agent locates no source satisfying every constraint and explicitly declines. For example, it reports it “could not find a single person who satisfies all parts of your query” for the gold answers Kathryn Stack Morgan and Laura Lojo-Rodríguez. Forcing an answer suppresses clarification requests but does not induce fabrication: the model still abstains honestly when retrieval fails, and the abstention is scored as incorrect.

  • ∙\bullet

    Wrong entity committed: 30/6330/63 the agent locks onto a specific candidate that satisfies a subset of the clues but is not the target, and cites a source for it (all 30 are grounded in at least one citation). For example, it names the artist Amaarae (Ama Serwah Genfi) when the requested birth name was Emmanuel Kwesi Danso Arthur Junior.

This contrasts with the LOONG failure mode (§ E.2): there the agent finds the correct entity but extracts the wrong figure, whereas on BrowseComp+ the entity itself is wrong or unfound. The difference stems from the task: BrowseComp+ requires satisfying many constraints jointly across the entire public web, so without the curated corpus that contains the annotated evidence document, the agent either surfaces no source meeting every constraint or commits to a partial match.

Appendix F Closed-Book Ablation and Correctness Decomposition

Fig. 5shows that answer correctness exceeds recall on LOONG L2 and KILT-HotpotQA, but not on BrowseComp+. To determine whether these gaps reflect the synthesizer compensating with parametric knowledge, or simply reflect questions that do not require complete retrieval to answer, we run a closed-book ablation: the same synthesizer model and prompt template as the main pipeline, but with the retrieved context entirely removed.

Setup.

We evaluate two closed-book conditions per dataset, both using the same synthesizer model (gpt-5-mini) and the same structured output schema as the main pipeline, but differing in what the synthesizer is told and given.

no-guess is the pipeline’s default synthesizer prompt, run with the context field emptied:

System: You are a helpful assistant that answers questions based on the provided context.
User: Instructions:
1. Based on the following context answer the question.
2. Do not use any other information or your internal knowledge to answer the question.
3. If required information is not present in the context, reply correspondingly with “Not enough context”
Query: {query}
Context: (empty)

Because this prompt explicitly instructs the model not to use its own knowledge, it measures the leak floor: how often the model answers by disregarding that instruction, given nothing else to go on.

best-guess uses a separate prompt that instructs the model to answer from its own knowledge instead of declining:

System: You are a helpful assistant. Answer the question using your own knowledge. Be concise and give the specific answer.
User: {question}
If you do not know the answer, reply exactly: I don’t know.

This measures the parametric ceiling: the upper bound of what the model could answer from memory alone when explicitly asked to. Both conditions are scored with the same correctness metric used throughout the paper.

The gap between them is informative in its own right: a low no-guess score paired with a high best-guess score indicates the model holds latent knowledge of the answer.

Results.

Table 9 reports no-guess and best-guess correctness alongside full-pipeline correctness, for all four benchmarks.

No-guess correctness is 0.00 on every benchmark: without being pushed to guess, the synthesizer never volunteers a confident, correct answer from memory alone under this instruction. This alone would suggest “no parametric leakage under no context,” but it understates the model’s latent knowledge, since a model can hold information it is unwilling to assert outright.

Best-guess correctness reveals the actual spread: near zero on LOONG (both levels) and BrowseComp+, but 0.67 on KILT. This splits the four benchmark–level pairs into two groups: memory-free (LOONG, BrowseComp+), where the model has no usable latent knowledge of the answer, and parametric-dominated (KILT), where most of the pipeline’s correctness is already recoverable without any retrieval at all.

LOONG L2: partial sufficiency, not memory.

With best-guess correctness near zero, the 17 of 50 L2 queries that are answered correctly despite incomplete recall (§ 4.2) cannot be explained by memory. Manual inspection of these 17 shows two distinct patterns:

  • ∙\bullet

    12 of 17: the winning company’s document was at least partially retrieved (its name surfaced in context) but mostly not its value, let alone the full candidate set. The synthesizer landed the comparison from the winner’s name alone, without the deciding evidence itself.

  • ∙\bullet

    5 of 17: the winning company was absent from the retrieved text entirely — answered correctly purely from a rankable/robust partial subset (or luck). For example, given a question of the form “among candidate companies {A1,…,AnA_{1},\dots,A_{n}}, which had the highest [metric]?” with gold winner CirTran Corp, 0 of the 2 companies actually needed to resolve the comparison were retrieved, yet the answer was still correct. Because the answer space is constrained to the small set of candidates named in the question itself, a correct answer here does not imply access to the correct underlying values. Instead, it can reflect the model recovering the right choice from an incomplete or even empty comparison set, which we term order-robust guessing.

Because best-guess closed-book correctness on LOONG L2 is near zero, this pattern cannot be attributed to parametric memory of the underlying financial figures: the model provably does not know these values unprompted.

KILT: shortcut and memory, entangled.

KILT’s high best-guess ceiling (0.67) reflects that HotpotQA questions, being sourced from Wikipedia, are frequently answerable from general knowledge. Of the 34 of 100 queries answered correctly despite incomplete recall, we distinguish two patterns by whether the answer text is present anywhere in the retrieved context:

  • •

    26 of 34: the answer text is present in the retrieved context, even though not every annotated bridge hop was fetched. This matches a well-documented artifact of the HotpotQA dataset, where many nominally multi-hop questions can be solved via a single-hop shortcut. For example, match salient entities in the question directly against a single retrieved passage without connecting the intermediate bridge [34, 27]. For example, the question “What film stars Rose McGowan and features the character of Earl McGraw’s daughter?” (gold answer: Planet Terror) was answered correctly with only 1 of 3 annotated hops retrieved, because the answer text itself was present in what was retrieved.

  • •

    8 of 34: the answer text is absent from all retrieved content, yet the query is answered correctly. For example: “Who narrated the 26-episode series featuring the British national museum …?” (gold answer: Michael Redgrave) and “’Hold On’ features a British singer whose debut album won what prize?” (gold answer: Mercury Prize), both answered correctly with 0 of 4 annotated hops retrieved and no occurrence of the answer text in retrieved content. Here the final hop is never fetched at all, and the answer is supplied from parametric memory.

Summary.

Table 10 restates the three mechanisms identified in § 4.2 against the ablation evidence supporting each.

Appendix G Prompts

For reproducibility, we list the exact prompts used at each pipeline stage. All prompts use gpt-5-mini unless otherwise noted, and all synthesizer-facing prompts (synthesis, closed-book conditions) use the same structured output schema (answer, relevant_context_present).

Query processing.

Query decomposition and rephrasing uses a fixed template with structured output into a TransformedQuery object (queries, query_rephrased, query_decomposed). In our benchmark runs this is computed once per query and cached, so the same decomposition is reused across all values of kk in the sweep in footnote 8.

System: You are a helpful assistant that transforms user queries for websearch using the provided instructions
User: Instructions:
1. Rephrase the query, IF AND ONLY IF, the current phrasing would not be good for search on a web search engine
2. IF it is a complex query, decompose it into a list of simpler web search queries that can provide the data necessary to answer the query
3. If the query was rephrased at all from the original query, set query_rephrased to true
4. If the query was decomposed, set query_decomposed to true
USER QUERY:
{query}

Synthesis (main pipeline).

The synthesizer’s answer-generation prompt ( in Fig. 2) is identical to the no-guess closed-book prompt ( Appendix F), with one difference: the context field is populated with the retrieved chunks rather than left empty.

Closed-book: no-guess.

See  Appendix F.

Closed-book: best-guess.

See  Appendix F.

Web-search agent baseline

Both configurations use gpt-5-mini with the OpenAI Responses web_search tool; they differ only in whether the tool is forced and whether the no-memory instruction is prepended to the question.

Autonomous: tool_choice left at default (the model decides whether to search); the question is passed as-is, with no instruction prepended.
User: <question>

Search-only (no memory): tool_choice forces the web_search tool on every call; the following instruction is prepended to the question.
User: You are a web-search answering agent. You MUST use the web_search tool to look up the answer, and you must answer using ONLY information found in the retrieved web results. Do NOT rely on prior or parametric knowledge. Do NOT ask for clarification: if the question is ambiguous, choose the most reasonable interpretation and commit to a single, specific final answer. Be concise.
Question: <question>

In both configurations, the agent’s final message is taken directly as the answer, with no separate synthesis step.

Contextual chunking (+ctx) document summary.

At ingest, the +ctx variant generates one summary per document, cached per document and prepended verbatim to every chunk of that document.

System: You produce short retrieval-oriented context snippets. Answer only with the requested context or summary.
User: <document>
{document}
</document>
Please give a short succinct summary of this document that can be added to each chunk of this document for the purposes of improving search retrieval of the chunks of this document.
Answer only with the summary and nothing else.

Evaluation: closed-ended benchmarks.

We score LOONG, KILT-HotpotQA, and BrowseComp+ with a single GEval metric, GoldCorrectness, over (INPUT, ACTUAL_OUTPUT, EXPECTED_OUTPUT):

Assess whether ACTUAL_OUTPUT is correct relative to EXPECTED_OUTPUT for INPUT. Use EXPECTED_OUTPUT as the authoritative reference answer and the sole basis for correctness judgment. Compare the meaning of ACTUAL_OUTPUT against EXPECTED_OUTPUT. Do not use outside knowledge, real-world plausibility, or independent fact-checking to override or dispute EXPECTED_OUTPUT. Allow harmless differences in formatting, punctuation, capitalization, commas, spacing, and minor unit wording when the underlying answer meaning is unchanged. Accept missing currency symbols when the value and meaning still clearly match EXPECTED_OUTPUT, but treat a different or implied different currency as incorrect. Treat currency meaning and numeric sign as semantically important. Accept equivalent negative-number notation such as a leading minus sign, accounting-style parentheses, or clearly equivalent wording like a loss. Accept extra explanation if the core answer remains clearly correct and is not contradicted.

This single metric is a semantic match against the gold answer, lenient on formatting and currency notation but strict on numeric sign and currency identity.

Evaluation: open-ended benchmark ( Appendix D).

The open-ended benchmark has no single gold answer, so we score each response along three separate GEval metrics over (INPUT, ACTUAL_OUTPUT) only — no expected output:

Correctness (GoldCorrectness): Assess whether ACTUAL_OUTPUT is factually correct and relevant to INPUT. [Judge] based on real-world plausibility and internal consistency. Penalize factual errors, fabricated claims, and contradictions. Do not require matching a [reference answer].
Completeness (QueryCompleteness): Assess how completely ACTUAL_OUTPUT answers the INPUT query by itself. [Reward covering all] essential requested points and penalize omissions of key parts of the question. Ignore stylistic differences.
Focus (Focus): Assess how focused ACTUAL_OUTPUT is on INPUT. Higher score means the response is [concise], precise, and relevant to the query. Penalize digressions, unnecessary tangents, and irrelevant details.

The dashed reference line in  Fig. 6 is Opus’s own gold answers, scored as ACTUAL_OUTPUT against these same three prompts.
